editorial.text: First off, thanks to the Library Campaign who made me an offer I could not refuse to restart Public Libraries News. This is incredibly generous and a big thank you to them for allowing this somewhat unique newsletter/website to come alive again. Of course, nothing in life is free so if you are in a position to offer advertising or other sponsorship on this site do let me know. However, as one door (re)opens, another door closes. Much to the surprise of many public librarians, LibraryOn, which was the ACE-funded and British Library-run website result of a decade-plus effort to have a “Single Digital Presence” for public libraries, has come to the end of its funding and will cease this week. There will be a report on how well it did published later this year. The site was a unique national shopfront for libraries. However, one could argue it was a shop window with no stock: there was no direct way to search for a book, an eBook or an eResource, for instance, although there was an interesting attempt at listing library events. That may be due to the nature of the beast. The multitude of library services were never going to agree to combine into one webpage or to agree one national eBook service without an almighty push or incentive. I hope, though, that it does not take another decade to get things moving again. News from a few Reform controlled library services this week makes it clear that they want politically neutral displays and events. Unfortunately, the list of what is accepted – Armed Forces Day, St George’s Day, anything to do with the Royal Family – shows that this means it should only be on things Reform agrees with. So, goodbye to displays or events to do with refugees or Black History Month or any non-Christian religious festival or anything LGBTQ. Before Reform, library services had been used to doing their own displays and events policies with the normal understanding that they’d just be nodded through. Not any more. Rejoice for you now have councillors who care about what you do. Or at the very least keep your heads down, as one suspects library staff are doing, for there is nothing you can do about this locally unless you want to put your job in danger. And, for goodness sake, take down that book on display about the history of the RNLI.
